newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine cement sector outlook seen bright.
newsitem.headline: Philippine cement sector outlook seen bright.

text.p: The outlook for the Philippine cement industry is bright and market expectations of a glut are unfounded, Manila stock brokerages said on Monday.
"The country's cement industry will continue to experience tight supply through 1998," Peregrine Capital Philippines said in a study.
"Contrary to market expectations of a glut, the cement industry's outlook will remain favourable amid the surge in infrastructure development and the unmet demand for housing," it said.
A separate recommendation released by brokerage Dharmala Securities on Monday said: "Cement sector - Accumulate".
"With money flowing out of property issues, the cement sector will likely receive buying interest from fund managers looking for quality issues with reasonable valuations,"Dharmala said.
"These laggard stocks are trading at attractive levels given a 1997 weighted average EPS growth of 69 percent and a sectoral multiple of 10.7 times next year's earnings."

Dharmala said concerns about a glut were raised by a cement manufacturers' association forecast of 106 million excess bags in the domestic market in 1998 when many new capacities are scheduled to come on line.
The forecast was based on the assumption that Apo Cement and Premiere Cement will start commercial operations by 1998 and Southern Cross and South Western by 1999, Dharmala said.
The brokerage said all, except one, were new cement plants in the ground-breaking stage. Also demand would continue to remain strong, it said.
The present government was fast-tracking the construction of several vital infrastructure projects and demand was bound to grow rapidly, it said.
The Peregrine study said conventional market estimates of cement demand have been based on a "simplistic assumption of a straight 15 percent historical growth rate."

The brokerage, citing its own study, said future Philippine cement demand would grow at an average of 19 percent until the year 2000 and will be the strongest before the end of President Fidel Ramos's term in 1998.
Peregrine said the large unfulfilled demand for housing as well as infrastructure projects pursued by the Ramos government would push cement demand.
